content.title: Computers are extremely literal
content.body:
Computers follow instructions exactly as they are written. Not what you meant. Not what you were thinking. Exactly what you told them to do.

If you say "open the fridge and get the milk" but forget to say "close the fridge," a robot might leave the fridge open because you never told it to close it.

This isn't a flaw — it's just how computers work. Once you understand that, writing good code becomes much easier.

content.title: Order matters — every time
content.body:
Computers follow instructions from top to bottom, in the exact order you write them.

If you write:
  1. Pour the juice
  2. Open the bottle

...the computer tries to pour from a closed bottle. It doesn't rearrange the steps or use common sense. It simply follows the order you gave it.

content.title: Try the robot test
content.body:
When you're not sure if your instructions are clear enough, imagine a robot that can only follow instructions literally — no guessing, no filling in gaps.

Would your instructions make sense to that robot? If yes, they'll probably make sense to a computer too.

Many bugs happen because instructions are missing, unclear, or in the wrong order.

content.title: This is why bugs exist
content.body:
A bug is a mistake in a program that makes it behave unexpectedly.

Many beginner bugs come from:

• A missing step
• Steps in the wrong order
• A typo
• Forgetting to handle a situation you didn't think about

Bugs don't mean you're bad at programming — they mean you're programming. Every programmer writes bugs. The important skill is learning how to find and fix them.

content.title: Computers are great at repetition
content.body:
Computers are very good at repeating instructions quickly and accurately.

A human might get bored counting every coin in a giant treasure pile. A computer can repeat the same steps thousands or millions of times without getting tired.

Later, you'll learn how programmers tell computers to repeat instructions automatically.

content.title: Algorithms: your plan for solving a problem
content.body:
An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step plan for solving a problem.

For example, imagine you want to find the highest score on a game leaderboard:

  1. Start by assuming the first score is the highest
  2. Look at each score one at a time
  3. If you find a higher score, replace the current best
  4. After checking all the scores, the highest one wins

The important part is the idea: programmers think through a clear plan before writing code.

quiz.question: If your instructions are unclear, a computer will try to figure out what you meant.
quiz.explanation: Correct. Computers follow instructions exactly as written. They don't guess what you meant.

quiz.question: Your robot instructions say: "1. Pour the juice. 2. Open the bottle." What happens?

options.text: The robot pours the juice successfully
The robot opens the bottle first because it's smart
The robot tries to pour from a closed bottle
The robot asks you to explain

quiz.explanation: The robot follows the instructions in order. Since the bottle wasn't opened yet, it tries to pour from a closed bottle.

quiz.question: What is a bug in a program?

options.text: A real insect inside a computer
A mistake in the code that causes problems
A program that is too long
A computer running out of battery

quiz.explanation: A bug is a mistake in a program that makes it behave in a way the programmer didn't expect.

quiz.question: Why are computers good at repetition?

options.text: They never get bored or tired of repeating steps

quiz.explanation: Computers can repeat instructions extremely quickly and accurately without getting tired.

quiz.question: What is an algorithm?

options.text: A precise, step-by-step plan for solving a problem

quiz.explanation: An algorithm is a clear plan for solving a problem step by step.
